# bayesEfron <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="bayesEfron hex sticker" />

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/joonho112/bayesEfron/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/joonho112/bayesEfron/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

A meta-analysis or a multisite trial gives an estimate and a standard error
for each site. The usual random-effects model assumes that the true effects
behind the estimates follow a normal distribution. bayesEfron fits the same
model without that assumption. It estimates the distribution of true
effects, which may be skewed or have more than one peak, together with the
effect of each site. The distribution is represented by Efron's log-spline
family and the model is fully Bayesian, so that the intervals for the site
effects include the uncertainty about the distribution
([Lee and Sui, 2025](https://doi.org/10.3390/math13162639)).

## Installation

You can install bayesEfron from GitHub with:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("joonho112/bayesEfron")
```

The vignettes are on the
[package website](https://joonho112.github.io/bayesEfron/). To install them
with the package, you need knitr, rmarkdown and Pandoc (RStudio includes
Pandoc). Then add `build_vignettes = TRUE` to the call above.

Fitting a model also requires the cmdstanr package and CmdStan, neither of
which is on CRAN:

```{r install-cmdstan, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev", getOption("repos")))
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()
```

CmdStan is built from source and needs a C++ toolchain. Use
`cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain()` to check whether you have one. The cmdstanr
[Getting started article](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html)
describes the installation and points to the requirements for each
operating system. The bayesEfron examples and vignettes run without
CmdStan.

## Example

The data set `krw_discrimination` contains estimates for 97 large U.S.
firms from the correspondence experiment of
[Kline, Rose and Walters (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjac024). For
each firm, `yi` is the difference between the callback rates of job
applications with distinctively white and distinctively Black names, and
`sei` is its standard error, clustered by job vacancy. A positive gap
favors applications with white names, and 0.02 is a gap of 2 percentage
points. The sample follows the authors'
[2024 analysis](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20230700), and the estimates
come from the public replication code that accompanies
[Walters (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/bs.heslab.2024.11.001).
[Lee and Sui (2025)](https://doi.org/10.3390/math13162639) analyze these
data with this model.

```{r data}
library(bayesEfron)
head(krw_discrimination[, c("firm_name", "yi", "sei")], 3)
```

We fit the model with `bayes_efron_fit()`. This call requires CmdStan, and
the first call compiles the Stan program, which can take up to a minute.

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
dat <- as_bef_data(krw_discrimination, site = "firm_name")
fit <- bayes_efron_fit(dat, seed = 20250807)
```

The result of this call is included in the package as `krw_fit` (thinned
to 800 draws), so the rest of the example runs without CmdStan.

```{r stored-fit}
fit <- krw_fit
fit
```

`g_summary()` summarizes the distribution of the gaps across firms. Here we
ask for its mean, variance and standard deviation on the percentage-point
scale, and for the proportion of firms with a positive gap. Each row has a
posterior mean and a 90% posterior interval.

```{r g-summary}
g_summary(fit, type = "moments", scale = 100)
g_summary(fit, type = "prob", lower = 0)
```

`site_summary()` returns posterior summaries of the gap at each firm, and
`exceedance_prob()` the posterior probability that a gap is positive.

```{r sites}
sites <- site_summary(fit, scale = 100)
head(sites[, c("label", "estimate", "se", "mean", "lower", "upper")], 4)
exceedance_prob(fit, sites = c("Rite Aid", "KFC"))
```

Finally, we plot the estimated distribution together with the normal
distribution of a random-effects model.

```{r callback-gaps, fig.alt = "The estimated density of the callback gaps of 97 firms in percentage points, with its 90% band, and the dashed curve of a normal distribution fitted to the same estimates."}
plot_g(fit, normal = TRUE, scale = 100) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "White-minus-Black callback gap (percentage points)")
```

The solid curve is the posterior mean of the density of the gaps, and the
band is a pointwise 90% posterior interval. The dashed curve is the normal
distribution of the usual random-effects model, with its mean and standard
deviation estimated by restricted maximum likelihood and shown without
their uncertainty. The model is free to depart from the normal shape, and
the band shows how well the data determine that shape: better in the
center, where the band is narrow relative to the height of the curve, than
in the tails.

## A distribution with two groups

`twin_towers` is a simulated data set of 1,500 sites from the public
replication files of Lee and Sui (2025), in which the true effects form
two groups. In `vignette("twin-towers")` we fit it with the grid chosen
from the estimates alone, as we would for real data, and compare the
result with the true effects.

<img src="man/figures/twin-towers.png" alt="The estimated density of the effects of 1,500 simulated sites with its band, a histogram of the true effects in two groups, and the dashed curve of a normal distribution." width="100%" />

The largest standard error is nine times the smallest, and for about one
site in seven it is larger than the gap between the two groups. The fitted
density has a peak over each group and little mass between them, which a
normal distribution, with its single peak, cannot have. This is a single
data set; see `vignette("implementation")` for how often the 90% intervals
contain the true effects across simulated data sets, including the
settings in which their coverage falls short of 90%.

## Learning more

- [Getting started with bayesEfron](https://joonho112.github.io/bayesEfron/articles/bayesEfron.html)
  walks through the analysis of the 97 firms, from preparing the data to
  summarizing the results.
- [Choosing the grid and checking sensitivity to it](https://joonho112.github.io/bayesEfron/articles/choosing-a-grid.html)
  discusses how the results can depend on the grid.
- [Checking a fit](https://joonho112.github.io/bayesEfron/articles/diagnostics.html)
  covers the diagnostics.

The [package website](https://joonho112.github.io/bayesEfron/) lists the
other vignettes. It also has a case study that is not installed with the
package: the effect of small classes in the 79 schools of Tennessee's
Project STAR, a multisite trial in education. The estimates for that case
study are in `star_schools`.

## Citation

To cite the package, cite the paper, as `citation("bayesEfron")` shows:

> Lee, J. and Sui, D. (2025). Fully Bayesian inference for meta-analytic
> deconvolution using Efron's log-spline prior. *Mathematics*, 13(16), 2639.
> <https://doi.org/10.3390/math13162639>
